title: Recursive Self-Improvement in AI
one_line_claim: Self-improvement is only as real as its verification: strength tracks a hierarchy from formal proofs down to a model's own confidence.

mechanism_steps.label: Bounded loop
mechanism_steps.detail: The system improves against a fixed external evaluator, not its own definition of better.
mechanism_steps.narration: Most self-improving systems run a bounded loop. They improve against a fixed external evaluator, not their own idea of what counts as better.

mechanism_steps.label: Evaluator
mechanism_steps.detail: Every loop is a claim that some signal can substitute for human judgment.
mechanism_steps.narration: Every loop rests on an evaluator. The system is only as good as whatever decides what counts as an improvement.

mechanism_steps.label: Hierarchy
mechanism_steps.detail: Signal reliability rises from a model's own confidence up to a formal proof.
mechanism_steps.narration: Evaluators sit on a hierarchy. Formal proofs are strongest, then tests, then learned judges, then the model's own confidence, weakest of all.

mechanism_steps.label: Failure modes
mechanism_steps.detail: Self-confirming loops, model collapse, and reward hacking follow from skipping a rung.
mechanism_steps.narration: Skip a rung and the loop breaks. Self-confirming loops, model collapse, and reward hacking all follow from that.

application_or_implication: Use the verification hierarchy to choose stronger evaluators before an agent accepts its own changes.
limits_or_caveats: The paper does not claim recursive self-improvement is running inside frontier labs today; industrial practice is only observable through what labs choose to publish.
street_test_question: Does your last self-improving pipeline climb the verification hierarchy, or does it just trust its own confidence?
